First, we substitute $u={x}^{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2x\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{2}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }2x\cdot {7}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{7}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }2x\cdot {7}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{7}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{7}^{-u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡7}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡7}{lim}_{a\to \infty }[{7}^{-u}]_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡7}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{{7}^{a}}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡7}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{7}^{a}})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{7}^{x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{7}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{7}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14260591/assets/c92f73e6a4932584f606118dc45b0573a863634bffa27a07ef0e8e17a411e38b.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }2x\cdot {7}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡7}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{7}^{a}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡7}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡7}.\end{aligned}
$$
